data.title: Shadow
data.tagline: Use light and depth to separate overlapping surfaces
data.description: A shadow can show that a menu, dialog, or card sits above another surface. It should support a real layer relationship, not decorate every box. A small, consistent shadow scale is easier to read than many unrelated effects.

use: Lift a floating menu above the page
Separate a dialog from its backdrop
Show an elevated card on a similar background
Build a small set of depth levels
avoid: Add a strong shadow to every container
Use several shadow directions on the same page
Rely on shadow alone when contrast is too low
Make a flat item look clickable when it is not

lessonPractice.title: A page has regular cards, dropdowns, and a modal, but every element uses the same heavy shadow. How should hierarchy become clearer?

options.label: Keep ordinary content restrained, strengthen shadows by actual elevation, and use one light direction
options.feedback: Shadow differences map to interface elevation, while consistent direction makes the layers belong to one system.

options.label: Keep heavy shadows on every card and control so each element stands out
options.feedback: When everything floats, relative hierarchy disappears and many competing boundaries fill the page.

options.label: Add the same shadow to body text to improve contrast against light surfaces
options.feedback: Text shadow reduces glyph clarity; foreground and background colors should establish readable contrast.

data.agentPrompt: Create a consistent shadow hierarchy: keep regular cards mostly flat, use light elevation for dropdowns and popovers, and a clearer but restrained modal shadow with one direction. Never shadow body text; test light and dark surfaces.
